extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for applying, combining, and assessing approximate generalizations, probabilities, resemblances, and existence-claims in inductive and scientific reasoning. Includes when approximations may be treated as universal and how mathematical/ geometrical truths fit into inductive logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying an approximate generalization to an individual case
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'Most A are B' has been established by sufficient induction, we may conclude that any particular A is a B with a probability proportioned to the preponderance of affirmative instances over exceptions; numerical precision can be given when practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only valid within the limits of time, place, and circumstance embraced in the observations; do not apply the genus-average to a known species/sub-class or to cases under conditions not included in the average. A general average should be applied only to cases which are neither known nor can be presumed to be other than average cases (e.g., life tables helpful for large numbers but weak for an individual's life). Subsequent approximations should incorporate particular circumstances of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining independent approximate generalizations by addition
rubrics_metrics.description: When two approximate generalizations are each separately applicable to the same case, combining them (addition) yields a probability greater than either alone (the probabilities cooperate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute combined probability by considering complements and independence (example: if 2/3 of As are Bs and 3/4 of Cs are Bs, then among things both A and C, 11/12 are B). This assumes the probabilistic contributions from each generalization are independent—use multiplication of complementary probabilities to derive the joint exception rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining approximate generalizations by deduction (chain reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: When only one proposition directly applies and another applies only by virtue of the first (a chain: Most A are B; Most B are C), the degree of probability of the final inference diminishes at each deductive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The resulting probability is typically less than either premise; measure it by multiplying the proportions (e.g., nine-tenths × eight-ninths = four-fifths). Ensure the second generalization was taken fairly with reference to the first (no biased distribution of B within A). Long chains rapidly erode probability; avoid relying on multi-step hearsay ('a hearsay of a hearsay' is worthless after few removes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of independence when joining generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: When joining two generalizations by addition, it is supposed that the probabilities arising from each class are independent of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If membership in one class increases or decreases the chance of membership in the other (dependence), the straightforward combined-probability calculation is invalid. If exceptions overlap, the joint probability may be no greater than that arising from one generalization alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the length of probabilistic deduction chains
rubrics_metrics.description: Each step in a chain of deduction based on approximate generalizations diminishes the probability of the conclusion; the error of the conclusion aggregates the errors of the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless premises approach universal truth, after very few steps the conclusion may be of negligible value. Apply caution to inferences that rest on successive uncertain premises (e.g., testimony-of-testimony). Prefer short, well-founded chains or convert approximations into conditionals where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform approximations into universal propositions with explicit provisos
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reason we stop at an approximation is mere inconvenience and we can specify the distinguishing character of exceptions, we may rewrite an approximate proposition as a universal proposition with a proviso (condition) annexed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry the proviso forward through deductive steps so the conclusion becomes universal subject to explicit conditions; record each condition so the aggregate shows the accumulated limitations/errors (example: 'All persons who have uncontrolled power employ it ill, provided they are not persons of unusual strength of judgment and rectitude of purpose'). This permits long chains while keeping track of how the conclusion is qualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: When approximate generalizations function as universal truths in aggregate-level reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: In inquiries about properties of multitudes (e.g., politics, social science), what is true of most individuals often suffices as effectively universal for the mass or community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of policy or arrangements affecting large numbers, 'most' can be treated as 'all' because aggregate outcomes are determined by majority behavior; therefore approximate generalizations can be scientifically useful and practically reliable at the mass level even if they are not strictly universal for individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring existence from laws of succession or co-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence of an individual phenomenon, when not directly perceived, is inferred from inductive laws of succession or co-existence with known phenomena; general propositions of existence may be fully established by a single verified instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence-claims in logic refer to phenomena (perceptions or inferred possibilities of perception). To prove existence, show its connection by succession/co-existence with known things. A single positive instance can establish general existence (e.g., if one authenticated sighting of a sea-serpent occurred, it establishes existence in logical terms), subject to consideration of conditions under which it happens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining resemblance via direct juxtaposition or indirect comparison through a third
rubrics_metrics.description: Where direct comparison is practicable, resemblance is perceived by direct apprehension; when not practicable, compare each object with a third object (transportable standard) and reason from general propositions/formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect comparison is appropriate scientific process when direct juxtaposition is impossible or imprecise (example: compare two lines via a rule; use the general axiom 'things equal to the same thing are equal to one another'). Employ relevant laws of nature or mathematical axioms as the basis for such inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mathematical axioms and theorems as independent laws of resemblance and order
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical laws of equality, inequality, and proportionality are the principal uniformities of resemblance and order in place which can be treated independently of causation; they are inductive truths established by perpetual observation and direct apprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mathematical axioms as nearly universal (perception-based) premises for reasoning about resemblance and order; where mathematical relations are applicable, they provide infallible-seeming bases for deductions independent of the physical causes producing the phenomena (distinguish these from empirical equalities derived from causal laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the relation between order-in-place truths and causation, except in pure geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Most order-in-place facts (collocation of effects) are consequences of causal laws; only certain truths of geometry are independent of causation and can be treated like mathematical propositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inferring order in place, consider whether the order is a direct consequence of causal laws (and thus should be treated by causal induction) or whether it is a purely geometrical relation that can be reasoned about independently of physical origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt simple, uniform modes of definition (e.g., for numbers) to enable deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of numbers connote modes of formation (how aggregates are composed); selecting one simple, uniform mode of formation as the canonical connotation facilitates deductive derivation of other modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing uniform conventions (such as regarding each number as formed by adding a unit to the preceding number) simplifies reasoning and retention. Once a chain of inductive truths (modes of formation) connecting numbers is established, other relations can be deduced.
